title: Grounding Agent Memory: Environment-Probing Curation for Enterprise Agents

report.one_sentence: The paper addresses the failure of post-task memory curators to verify trajectory-derived lessons, and proposes giving an asynchronous curator agent read-only environment tools to check memories before committing them, reporting CLBench pass rate rising from 39% to 73% and task-agent cost falling from $3.38 to $1.68 versus a no-memory baseline.
report.problem: Post-task memory curation in agent systems operates only over completed trajectories, which are partial and mistake-laden observations of the environment; the resulting records can memorize instance answers, assert unverifiable scope, or go stale after environment drift, forcing the task agent to spend its budget re-verifying memory.
report.mechanism: The task agent, retriever, memory schema, and CRUD lifecycle are unchanged. After each task, a distiller compresses the raw trajectory, then a separate curator agent (the only memory writer) runs propose-probe-commit: it proposes candidate records, makes targeted read-only calls against the live environment (database queries or document/tool inspection) to verify correctness, scope, freshness, and procedure validity, then creates, narrows, updates, or deletes records. Probing adds only read-only tools and two prompt blocks to the curator; it runs off the task critical path and replaces task-time rediscovery with pre-validated memory.

evidence.claim: On CLBench (40-question drift schedule, GPT-5.4), environment-probed memory raises pass rate and reward over the no-memory baseline while reducing queries and cost.
evidence.result: Pass 39% to 73%, reward 8.60 to 22.60, queries 8.8 to 4.7/question, task-agent cost $3.38 to $1.68
evidence.conditions: GPT-5.4 task/distiller/curator, CLBench 40-question drift schedule, five paired seeded runs

evidence.result: Reward 20.00 to 22.60, queries 5.6 to 4.7, cost $1.99 to $1.68

evidence.claim: On the no-drift 30-question CLBench schedule, probing achieves the highest mean reward on both Sonnet 4.6 and Opus 4.7, exceeding both paired baselines and trajectory-only memory.
evidence.result: Sonnet 4.6: 0.748 vs 0.673 (Mem) and 0.327 baseline; Opus 4.7: 0.721 vs 0.696 and 0.458 baseline
evidence.baseline: Paired GHCP (No Memory) and GHCP + Mem per model
evidence.conditions: Fixed canonical 30-question no-drift order, five paired runs per model-memory comparison

evidence.claim: Across six adapted APEX worlds, all 18 memory-versus-baseline reward comparisons are positive and probing gives the best reward gain per task-agent dollar in five of six worlds.
evidence.result: All 18 gains positive; probing best reward/$ in 5 of 6 worlds; tool calls fall e.g. world 941eba66 from 71.6 to 19.3
evidence.conditions: GPT-5.4, 90 adapted APEX management-consulting tasks, five runs per stateful configuration

minimum_test: Pick one of your own workloads with a stream of 20-40 related tasks sharing latent environment structure (e.g., recurring database or document corpus), including at least one unannounced drift event, and define a strict pass/fail grader.

Stand up two memory pipelines that are identical in task agent, retriever, memory schema, distiller, and CRUD policy; give only one curator a least-privilege read-only subset of the environment tools plus the two probe prompt blocks from Appendix D.3.
Run both conditions plus a no-memory baseline on the same seeded task order with a small number of runs (at least 3 paired runs), keeping task agent, model, and prompts fixed.
Measure pass rate, task-agent tool calls, and task-agent cost, with curator/probe usage tracked separately; check whether probe curation calls stay read-only and off the task budget.

Inspect the committed memory records in both arms: if probed records are not more executable (explicit joins, paths, current schema) than trajectory-only records, the mechanism is not operating as claimed.
The reported gain is disproven for your workload if probing does not improve reward or tool-call count over trajectory-only memory, or if probing cost/latency erases the task-agent savings.
main_risks: All evaluation is on two benchmarks via a GitHub Copilot SDK harness; gains may not transfer to other agent stacks or task distributions.

The improvement over plain memory is modest and confidence intervals overlap in places; in one of six APEX worlds probing was slightly worse, and the authors explicitly treat heterogeneity as unresolved.
Requires a safe, least-privilege read-only environment surface for the curator; without one it degenerates to trajectory-only curation, and granting such access has security/auditing implications.
Curator, distiller, and probe costs are excluded from reported task-agent cost; total system cost including curation is not the headline metric and could offset savings.
Probing adds asynchronous compute after every task; latency and cost of the curation phase at production scale are not quantified in the main results.
Results depend on specific frontier models (GPT-5.4, Sonnet 4.6, Opus 4.7) and benchmark graders; weaker models may not probe effectively.
unanswered_questions: What is the total end-to-end cost including distiller and curator/probe sessions, which the paper says are tracked separately but does not headline?
How many probe calls does the curator typically make per task, and what governance prevents read-only probes from leaking information or being abused?
Does the gain persist on non-benchmark, messier enterprise environments where read-only surfaces are incomplete?
How sensitive are results to the curator prompt and to the embedding retriever (intfloat/e5-base-v2)?
Would probing help when memory errors come from retrieval failure rather than record quality, which this design does not address?
